timing_worsening_explanation: Symptoms tend to be worse in the morning, when Dampness is heaviest and the body is sluggish from overnight fluid accumulation. Damp weather and the late summer or early autumn (the season associated with the Spleen in the Five Phase system) can aggravate this pattern. The menstrual cycle itself is characteristically prolonged, with periods arriving later and later over time and potentially stopping altogether. Symptoms of heaviness, bloating, and discharge often worsen in the days before a period is expected, when the body's attempt to move blood meets the obstruction of Phlegm in the lower abdomen.
practitioner_notes:
Diagnosing Damp-Phlegm in the Uterus relies on recognizing the combination of menstrual disruption and signs of Phlegm-Dampness throughout the body. The practitioner looks for a cluster of clues: periods that come late, are scanty, or stop entirely, together with a heavier body type, copious white vaginal discharge, and a feeling of fullness or heaviness in the lower abdomen. These local reproductive symptoms must be accompanied by systemic signs that Phlegm and Dampness are present, such as chest stuffiness, nausea, a greasy tongue coating, and a slippery pulse.
The tongue is one of the most reliable diagnostic markers. A pale, swollen tongue body with visible teeth marks along the edges indicates that the Spleen is struggling. A white, greasy coating confirms that Dampness and Phlegm have accumulated internally. The slippery quality of the pulse further corroborates the presence of Phlegm. Together, these signs paint a clear picture of fluid metabolism gone wrong, with the turbid products settling in the lower abdomen and obstructing the uterus.
A key clinical pearl is the association between body habitus and menstrual irregularity. Classical texts note that when overweight women present with delayed or absent periods, Phlegm-Dampness obstruction should be the first consideration. This contrasts with thin women who have similar menstrual problems, where Blood Deficiency is more likely. The diagnostic logic follows directly from the pathology: excess body weight in this context is itself a manifestation of Phlegm accumulating in the tissues, and the same Phlegm that causes weight gain also blocks the Chong and Ren vessels that govern menstruation and fertility.
pathophysiology: The Spleen fails to properly transform body fluids, allowing Dampness to accumulate and thicken into Phlegm that sinks into the Uterus, obstructing the Chong and Ren vessels and disrupting menstruation and fertility.
treatment_principle: Dry Dampness and resolve Phlegm from the Uterus, strengthen the Spleen, and regulate menstruation
typical_timeline: 3-6 months for mild to moderate cases, 6-12 months or longer for severe or chronic cases with infertility. Phlegm is the most stubborn pathological substance in TCM and requires sustained treatment.
formula_modifications:
Common Formula Modifications for Cang Fu Dao Tan WanIf the person also feels very cold, especially in the lower abdomen and lower back: Add Rou Gui (Cinnamon Bark) and Wu Zhu Yu (Evodia Fruit) to warm the interior and help the Kidney Yang drive out Cold-Damp from the Uterus. Moxibustion on the lower abdomen is also recommended.
If the person feels very tired and low on energy with loose stools: Add Huang Qi (Astragalus) and Dang Shen (Codonopsis) to strongly tonify Spleen Qi. The Spleen must be strengthened at its root for lasting resolution of Dampness.
If there is a tendency toward Blood Stasis with stabbing lower abdominal pain and dark clots in the menstrual blood: Add Dang Gui (Chinese Angelica), Tao Ren (Peach Kernel), and Hong Hua (Safflower) to invigorate Blood and resolve stasis alongside the Phlegm.
If there is profuse white vaginal discharge that is thick and sticky: Add Hai Piao Xiao (Cuttlefish Bone) and Qian Shi (Euryale Seed) to astringe Dampness and firm up the Dai Mai (Girdle Vessel), which governs vaginal discharge.
If there are signs of Heat developing, such as yellow and smelly discharge or a yellow greasy tongue coating: Shift toward Huang Bai (Phellodendron Bark) and Yi Yi Ren (Coix Seed) to clear Damp-Heat, and reduce or remove warming herbs like Cang Zhu.
If the person is trying to conceive and ovulation is absent or irregular: Add Xian Ling Pi (Epimedium), Ba Ji Tian (Morinda Root), and Tu Si Zi (Cuscuta Seed) to warm Kidney Yang and promote ovulation. These address the root of reproductive function while the base formula clears the Phlegm obstruction.

causes_details: [{"cause_title": "Excessive consumption of greasy, sweet, or dairy-rich foods", "explanation": "The Spleen is the body's main digestive organ in TCM. It transforms food and drink into usable nutrients and manages fluids throughout the body. When a person regularly eats rich, greasy, sweet, or dairy-heavy foods, the Spleen becomes overwhelmed. These foods are difficult to fully process and leave behind a residue of unprocessed fluids. Over time, these fluids thicken and condense into what TCM calls Dampness, and eventually into Phlegm, a heavier, stickier pathological substance. Because fluids naturally tend to sink downward, this Damp-Phlegm settles into the Lower Burner (the pelvic region), where it blocks the Uterus and the vessels that nourish it."}, {"cause_title": "Spleen Qi deficiency from overthinking, overwork, or constitutional weakness", "explanation": "Even without a poor diet, the Spleen can become weakened through chronic stress, excessive mental work (which taxes the Spleen in TCM theory), physical exhaustion, or simply having been born with a weaker digestive constitution. When the Spleen lacks sufficient Qi to do its job, fluid metabolism slows down. Fluids that should be transformed and distributed instead pool and stagnate. This is why some women develop this pattern even with a reasonable diet: the problem is not what goes in, but the body's inability to process it efficiently. Over months and years, this gradual accumulation of poorly metabolised fluids congeals into Damp-Phlegm that settles in the Uterus."}, {"cause_title": "Kidney Yang deficiency failing to warm the Spleen", "explanation": "The Kidneys provide the foundational warmth (Yang) that all other organs depend on. TCM often uses the metaphor of a cooking pot: the Spleen is the pot that transforms food and fluids, and Kidney Yang is the fire underneath it. If Kidney Yang is insufficient, there is not enough heat to 'cook' the fluids properly. The Spleen becomes cold and sluggish, leading to Dampness accumulation. Because the Kidneys directly govern reproduction and the Uterus, this pathway is especially relevant in fertility-related presentations. As classical teaching states, 'the formation of Phlegm is from the Spleen, but the root of Phlegm lies in the Kidney.'"}, {"cause_title": "Liver Qi overacting on the Spleen", "explanation": "Emotional stress, frustration, or suppressed anger can cause the Liver's Qi to stagnate. In the Five Element cycle, the Liver (Wood) naturally controls the Spleen (Earth). When Liver Qi becomes excessive or stagnant, it can overpower the Spleen, impairing its transport and transformation functions. This is a very common pathway in women experiencing both emotional stress and menstrual irregularity. The stagnant Liver Qi disrupts Spleen function, Dampness forms, thickens into Phlegm, and descends to obstruct the Uterus."}, {"cause_title": "Sedentary lifestyle and lack of exercise", "explanation": "Physical movement helps Qi circulate throughout the body. When a person sits for long periods and rarely exercises, Qi and fluid circulation slows. Fluids that should be moving and transforming instead stagnate, particularly in the lower body and pelvic region. Over time, this stagnation creates a local environment that favours Dampness and Phlegm accumulation. This is why the pattern is commonly seen in women who have office jobs with prolonged sitting and limited physical activity."}, {"cause_title": "Living in a damp environment or exposure to external Dampness", "explanation": "External Dampness from the environment, such as living in a humid climate, a damp house, or being frequently exposed to wet and cold conditions, can penetrate the body and compound the internal tendency toward Dampness. The external pathogen combines with pre-existing internal weakness of the Spleen, accelerating the formation of Damp-Phlegm. This is especially common in regions with humid or rainy climates."}]

formulas.name: Cang Fu Dao Tan Wan
formulas.description: The primary formula for this pattern. Recorded in the Ye Shi Nü Ke Zheng Zhi (叶氏女科证治), it was designed specifically for overweight women with Phlegm obstruction causing amenorrhoea or infertility. It dries Dampness, resolves Phlegm, moves Qi, and regulates menstruation.

formulas.name: Er Chen Tang
formulas.description: The foundational Phlegm-resolving formula, forming the base of many modifications used in this pattern. It dries Dampness, transforms Phlegm, regulates Qi, and harmonises the Middle Burner.

formulas.name: Xiang Sha Liu Jun Zi Tang
formulas.description: Used when the underlying Spleen Qi deficiency is prominent. Strengthens the Spleen while resolving Dampness and moving Qi, particularly useful for late periods with Phlegm-Dampness.

formulas.name: Di Tan Tang
formulas.description: A stronger Phlegm-dispelling formula derived from Er Chen Tang with the addition of Zhi Shi and Dan Nan Xing. Suitable when Phlegm accumulation is heavy and stubborn.

formulas.name: Li Zhong Wan
formulas.description: Used when the focus is on restoring fertility by opening the Uterus. Combines Phlegm-resolving herbs with herbs that warm the Kidney and regulate the Chong and Ren vessels.

herbs.name: Cang Zhu
herbs.description: Strongly dries Dampness and strengthens the Spleen's ability to transform fluids. A key herb for eliminating the root cause of Phlegm accumulation.

herbs.name: Xiang Fu
herbs.description: Known as the 'commander of Qi among gynaecological herbs', it moves Qi, regulates menstruation, and helps Phlegm disperse by restoring smooth Qi flow.

herbs.name: Ban Xia
herbs.description: The premier herb for drying Dampness and dissolving Phlegm. Descends rebellious Stomach Qi and helps resolve nausea that often accompanies this pattern.

herbs.name: Chen Pi
herbs.description: Regulates Qi and dries Dampness, helping the Spleen recover its transport function. Works synergistically with Ban Xia to resolve Phlegm.

herbs.name: Fu Ling
herbs.description: Drains Dampness through gentle diuresis and strengthens the Spleen. Helps remove accumulated fluids without being overly drying.

herbs.name: Dan Nan Xing
herbs.description: A processed form of Tian Nan Xing that clears Heat and strongly dissolves stubborn Phlegm, particularly useful when Phlegm has congealed into masses.

herbs.name: Zhi Ke
herbs.description: Moves Qi and breaks up stagnation in the Middle Burner. Helps Qi circulate so that Phlegm can be dispersed rather than accumulating.

herbs.name: Chuan Xiong
herbs.description: Invigorates Blood and moves Qi, ensuring that Blood flow to the Uterus is restored once Phlegm obstruction begins to clear.

herbs.name: Yi Yi Ren
herbs.description: Strengthens the Spleen while draining Dampness. Gentle enough for long-term use and supports the Spleen's role in preventing further Phlegm formation.

herbs.name: Bai Zhu
herbs.description: Tonifies Spleen Qi and dries Dampness. Addresses the underlying Spleen weakness that allows Phlegm to form in the first place.

acupoints.name: Zhongji REN-3
acupoints.description: The Front-Mu point of the Bladder, located on the Ren Mai just above the pubic bone. Directly regulates the Uterus and Lower Burner, resolves Dampness, and restores menstrual flow.

acupoints.name: Guanyuan REN-4
acupoints.description: Tonifies Kidney Qi and warms the Lower Burner. Strengthens the body's ability to transform and expel Damp-Phlegm from the reproductive area.

acupoints.name: Fenglong ST-40
acupoints.description: The Luo-Connecting point of the Stomach channel and the single most important acupuncture point for resolving Phlegm anywhere in the body. Essential for this pattern.

acupoints.name: Sanyinjiao SP-6
acupoints.description: The meeting point of the three Yin channels of the leg (Spleen, Liver, Kidney). Regulates menstruation, strengthens the Spleen, and resolves Dampness. A key point for virtually all gynaecological conditions.

acupoints.name: Yinlingquan SP-9
acupoints.description: The He-Sea point of the Spleen channel. Strongly resolves Dampness from the Lower Burner and supports the Spleen's fluid-transforming function.

acupoints.name: Zusanli ST-36
acupoints.description: The He-Sea point of the Stomach channel. Powerfully tonifies Spleen and Stomach Qi, which is the root treatment for preventing further Phlegm generation.

acupoints.name: Zhongwan REN-12
acupoints.description: The Front-Mu point of the Stomach and the Influential point for the Fu organs. Strengthens the Middle Burner's digestive function to address the source of Dampness and Phlegm production.

acupoints.name: Qihai REN-6
acupoints.description: Tonifies Qi and warms the lower abdomen. Supports the body's overall Qi to help mobilise and transform stagnant Dampness in the pelvic area.

faqs.question: What is Damp-Phlegm in the Uterus in TCM?
faqs.answer: The Spleen fails to properly transform body fluids, allowing Dampness to accumulate and thicken into Phlegm that sinks into the Uterus, obstructing the Chong and Ren vessels and disrupting menstruation and fertility.

faqs.question: What are the key signs of Damp-Phlegm in the Uterus?
faqs.answer: Key signs include: Periods arriving late or stopping entirely, Scanty menstrual flow when periods do occur, Profuse thick white vaginal discharge, Weight gain or obesity, Lower abdominal fullness and heaviness, Difficulty conceiving, Chest stuffiness, Nausea or tendency to feel queasy, Feeling of heaviness in the whole body, Fatigue and drowsiness, Poor appetite, Loose or sticky stools, Dull pale complexion.

faqs.question: What formulas treat Damp-Phlegm in the Uterus?
faqs.answer: Common formulas for Damp-Phlegm in the Uterus include: Cang Fu Dao Tan Wan, Er Chen Tang, Xiang Sha Liu Jun Zi Tang, Di Tan Tang, Li Zhong Wan.

faqs.question: What Western conditions relate to Damp-Phlegm in the Uterus?
faqs.answer: This pattern is associated with: Polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS), Infertility (female), Amenorrhoea, Oligomenorrhoea, Ovarian cysts, Uterine fibroids, Uterine polyps, Obesity with menstrual irregularity, Excessive vaginal discharge (leukorrhoea), Anovulation, Fallopian tube obstruction.

faqs.question: What is the treatment principle for Damp-Phlegm in the Uterus?
faqs.answer: Dry Dampness and resolve Phlegm from the Uterus, strengthen the Spleen, and regulate menstruation
